notes.definition: The transition metals are the elements in the central block of the periodic table, between Groups 2 and 3. They are metals with similar properties to each other, but compared with Group 1 metals they have much higher melting points and densities, are stronger and harder, and are much less reactive with oxygen, water and halogens.
explanation: The transition elements (transition metals) are found in the middle block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3. For GCSE you should know the examples chromium (Cr), manganese (Mn), iron (Fe), cobalt (Co), nickel (Ni) and copper (Cu), which are all in Period 4. They are all metals, so like the Group 1 metals they conduct electricity and heat, and they form positive ions. However, their physical and chemical properties are very different from those of the alkali metals.

Transition metals have much higher melting points than Group 1 metals. Iron melts at 1538 °C and chromium at 1907 °C, whereas sodium melts at only 98 °C and potassium at 63 °C. Copper, the lowest of the six examples, still melts at 1085 °C. This is why transition metals are solids that stay solid at high temperatures, while the alkali metals would melt in a hot oven.

Transition metals also have much higher densities. Iron has a density of 7.87 g/cm³ and copper 8.96 g/cm³, while lithium (0.53 g/cm³), sodium (0.97 g/cm³) and potassium (0.86 g/cm³) are less dense than water and float on it. Transition metals are much stronger and harder too: the alkali metals are soft enough to cut with a knife, but iron, nickel and chromium are hard and strong, which makes them useful as structural materials.

Transition metals are much less reactive than Group 1 metals. The alkali metals react quickly with oxygen at room temperature, tarnishing within seconds, while iron reacts with oxygen only slowly (it rusts slowly in the presence of oxygen and water), and copper only forms a black oxide when heated: 2Cu(s) + O₂(g) → 2CuO(s). Group 1 metals react vigorously with cold water to form hydroxides and hydrogen; iron reacts only very slowly and copper does not react with water at all.

With halogens the difference is similar. Sodium burns vigorously in chlorine to form sodium chloride, but iron needs to be heated strongly before it reacts with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride: 2Fe(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2FeCl₃(s). Copper reacts with chlorine only when heated. This low reactivity is why transition metals can be used in contact with air and water, for example copper in water pipes, while Group 1 metals must be stored under oil.

You should be able to use data to compare the two sets of metals and to explain uses. Because they are strong, hard, dense and slow to react, transition metals and their alloys are used for bridges, buildings, vehicles, tools, pipes and electrical wires. The Group 1 metals are too soft, too reactive and have melting points that are too low to be used as structural materials.
keyFacts: Transition metals are in the central block, between Groups 2 and 3.
Examples to know: chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel and copper.
Transition metals have much higher melting points than Group 1 metals (Fe 1538 °C v Na 98 °C).
Transition metals have much higher densities (Cu 8.96 g/cm³ v Na 0.97 g/cm³).
Transition metals are stronger and harder; Group 1 metals are soft and can be cut with a knife.
Transition metals react much less vigorously with oxygen, water and halogens.
Iron rusts slowly; copper does not react with water; sodium reacts vigorously with cold water.
Iron reacts with chlorine when heated: 2Fe(s) + 3Cl₂(g) → 2FeCl₃(s).
Both types are metals: both conduct electricity and heat and form positive ions.

keyTerms.definition: The metallic elements in the central block of the periodic table between Groups 2 and 3, such as iron and copper.
The Group 1 metals (lithium, sodium, potassium and so on), which are soft, low density and very reactive.
Mass per unit volume of a material, usually in g/cm³: density = mass ÷ volume.
The temperature at which a solid turns into a liquid.
How well a material resists being scratched or dented.
How well a material resists breaking when a force is applied.
How quickly and vigorously a substance takes part in chemical reactions.

equations.name: Density
equations.units: g/cm³ (mass in g, volume in cm³)

workedExamples.title: Calculating density
workedExamples.question: A rectangular block of iron measures 2.0 cm × 3.0 cm × 5.0 cm and has a mass of 236.1 g. Calculate the density of iron.

workedExamples.title: Comparing data
workedExamples.question: Copper has a density of 8.96 g/cm³ and sodium has a density of 0.97 g/cm³. How many times denser is copper than sodium?
steps: Divide the larger density by the smaller: 8.96 ÷ 0.97.

workedExamples.title: Using conservation of mass
workedExamples.question: 6.35 g of copper is heated in air until it has all reacted. 7.95 g of copper(II) oxide is formed. Calculate the mass of oxygen that reacted.
steps: Mass of oxygen = mass of copper oxide − mass of copper.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think all metals are hard, dense and have high melting points.
misconceptions.right: In fact Group 1 metals are soft, have low densities (they float on water) and low melting points. These properties are typical of transition metals, not all metals.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think transition metals do not react at all.
misconceptions.right: In fact they do react, but much more slowly than Group 1 metals. Iron rusts and reacts with chlorine when heated; copper forms an oxide when heated.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think transition metals are a group with a number, like Group 1.
misconceptions.right: In fact the transition metals are a block of many columns between Groups 2 and 3; they are not one numbered group.

realWorld: Iron, mainly as steel, is used for bridges, buildings and car bodies because it is strong, hard and has a high melting point.
Copper is used for water pipes because it does not react with water, and for electrical wiring because it conducts well.
Chromium is used to coat (chrome-plate) steel because it is hard and resists corrosion.
Nickel is used in coins and in stainless steel; sodium could never be used for these because it would react with moisture.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is for separate Chemistry (8462) only.
Transition metals compared with Group 1: higher melting points (except mercury), higher densities, greater strength and hardness, much less reactive with oxygen, water and halogens.
Examples to know: Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu.
examTips: Compare questions need both sides: for example 'iron has a much higher melting point than sodium', not just 'iron has a high melting point'.
Use data from the question to support each comparison, quoting numbers with units.
Cover all five properties named in the specification: melting point, density, strength, hardness and reactivity (with oxygen, water and halogens).
When linking to uses, explain why the property matters, for example 'high melting point so it stays solid in a hot engine'.
summary: Transition metals are in the central block between Groups 2 and 3.
They have much higher melting points and densities than Group 1 metals.
They are stronger and harder than the soft alkali metals.
They react much less vigorously with oxygen, water and halogens.
Examples: Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni and Cu, used for structures, pipes and wires.

flashcards.front: Where are the transition metals in the periodic table?
flashcards.back: In the central block, between Groups 2 and 3.

flashcards.front: Name the six transition metals you need to know.
flashcards.back: Chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel, copper.

flashcards.front: Compare melting points of transition metals and Group 1.
flashcards.back: Transition metals have much higher melting points (Fe 1538 °C, Na 98 °C).

flashcards.front: Compare densities of transition metals and Group 1.
flashcards.back: Transition metals are much denser (Cu 8.96 g/cm³, Na 0.97 g/cm³).
Transition metals are strong and hard; Group 1 metals are soft and can be cut with a knife.
Group 1 metals react vigorously with cold water; iron reacts very slowly, copper not at all.
Group 1 metals tarnish in seconds; iron rusts slowly; copper only forms an oxide when heated.
Sodium reacts vigorously; iron and copper react only when heated.

flashcards.front: Name two properties transition metals share with Group 1 metals.
flashcards.back: Both conduct electricity and heat, and both form positive ions.

flashcards.front: Why is copper used for water pipes but sodium is not?
flashcards.back: Copper does not react with water; sodium reacts vigorously with water.

markScheme: 1 mark: B
questions.explanation: The transition metals form the central block of the periodic table, between Group 2 and Group 3, which is region B. A is Group 1 (the alkali metals), C is Group 7 (the halogens) and D is Group 0 (the noble gases).

questions.question: Which of these elements is a transition metal?
markScheme: 1 mark: iron
questions.explanation: Iron is in the central block. Sodium is Group 1, calcium Group 2 and aluminium Group 3.

questions.question: Which property do transition metals have compared with Group 1 metals?
markScheme: 1 mark: higher melting points
questions.explanation: Transition metals have higher melting points and densities, are stronger, and are less reactive.

questions.question: Which property do the Group 1 metals and the transition metals share?
options: They can be cut with a knife
They react vigorously with cold water
markScheme: 1 mark: they conduct electricity
questions.explanation: Both are metals, so both conduct electricity. The other properties apply only to Group 1.

questions.question: Which of these metals would float on water?
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium
questions.explanation: Potassium's density (0.86 g/cm³) is less than water's (1.0 g/cm³). The transition metals are around 8 to 9 g/cm³.

questions.question: How does the reaction of copper with water compare with that of sodium?
options: Copper reacts more vigorously than sodium
Copper does not react, but sodium reacts vigorously
markScheme: 1 mark: copper no reaction, sodium vigorous
questions.explanation: Copper is very unreactive and does not react with water, which is why it is used for water pipes.

questions.question: Which is the correctly balanced equation for iron reacting with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride?
markScheme: 1 mark: 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃
questions.explanation: Iron(III) chloride is FeCl₃. Six chlorine atoms (3Cl₂) make two FeCl₃. Chlorine is always written as Cl₂.

questions.question: A metal is used to build a bridge. Which metal is most suitable?
options: Sodium, because it is a good conductor
Potassium, because it has a low density
Iron (as steel), because it is strong and hard
markScheme: 1 mark: iron, strong and hard
questions.explanation: Bridges need strong, hard, unreactive materials. Group 1 metals are soft and react with water and air.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows some information about a metal.
Which metal is it most likely to be?
markScheme: 1 mark: cobalt
questions.explanation: The high melting point, high density and low reactivity are typical transition metal properties. The Group 1 metals melt below 200 °C and react vigorously with water.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why sodium is stored under oil but iron is not?
options: Iron has a lower melting point than sodium
Sodium reacts quickly with oxygen and water vapour in air, but iron reacts only slowly
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium reacts quickly with air, iron slowly
questions.explanation: Sodium is much more reactive. Iron reacts slowly (rusting) so it can be left in air. Iron is denser and has a far higher melting point.

questions.question:

questions.question: Name one of the transition metals chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, nickel or copper that is used for electrical wiring.
markScheme: 1 mark: copper
questions.explanation: Copper is an excellent conductor, is ductile and does not react with water or air at room temperature.

questions.question: Give two physical properties in which transition metals differ from Group 1 metals.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: transition metals have higher melting points / higher densities / are stronger / are harder
questions.explanation: Each answer must be comparative, for example 'higher density', not just 'dense'.

questions.question: Compare the reactions of potassium and iron with cold water.
markScheme: 1 mark: potassium reacts vigorously with cold water (fizzes, melts, lilac flame, forms KOH and hydrogen)
1 mark: iron reacts only very slowly (it rusts slowly in water with oxygen) / hardly reacts
questions.explanation: A comparison needs statements about both metals.

questions.question: Compare how sodium and copper react with oxygen.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium reacts quickly with oxygen at room temperature / tarnishes in seconds
1 mark: copper reacts only when heated, slowly forming black copper(II) oxide
questions.explanation: Group 1 metals are far more reactive with oxygen than transition metals.

questions.question: Iron and sodium both react with chlorine. Describe how the reactions differ.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium reacts vigorously / burns brightly to form sodium chloride
1 mark: iron must be heated strongly and reacts less vigorously to form iron(III) chloride
questions.explanation: Both form metal chlorides, but the transition metal is much less reactive.

questions.question: Suggest why transition metals such as iron are used as structural materials but Group 1 metals are not.
markScheme: 1 mark: transition metals are strong and hard with high melting points
1 mark: Group 1 metals are soft and react quickly with water and oxygen in air, so would not last
questions.explanation: Both halves of the answer are needed: why iron is suitable and why Group 1 metals are not.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows information about two metals, A and B.
Identify which metal is a transition metal and which metal is in Group 1.
Give three pieces of evidence from Table 1.
markScheme: 1 mark: A is the transition metal and B is in Group 1
1 mark: A has a much higher melting point and density than B
1 mark: A is hard whereas B is soft (B would float on water)
questions.explanation: A is chromium and B is lithium. All three properties point the same way.

questions.question: Compare the properties of the transition metals with the properties of the Group 1 metals. Use examples in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: transition metals have much higher melting points (for example iron 1538 °C, chromium 1907 °C v sodium 98 °C, potassium 63 °C); higher densities (copper 8.96 g/cm³ v sodium 0.97 g/cm³; Group 1 metals float on water); stronger and harder (Group 1 can be cut with a knife); much less reactive with oxygen (Group 1 tarnish in seconds; iron rusts slowly; copper forms oxide only when heated); with water (Group 1 react vigorously forming hydroxides and hydrogen; iron very slowly; copper not at all); with halogens (sodium burns in chlorine; iron reacts only when heated, 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃); similarities: both metals, conduct electricity and heat, form positive ions.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison covering physical properties and reactivity with oxygen, water and halogens, with specific examples or data.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): several valid comparisons with some examples.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one type of metal, with little comparison.
questions.explanation: Each point should be a direct comparison supported by an example from Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni or Cu and from Li, Na or K.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows data for some metals.
A student claims that 'transition metals have higher melting points and higher densities than Group 1 metals'.
Evaluate this claim.
Use data from Table 1 in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: every transition metal in the table has a higher melting point than every Group 1 metal (lowest transition metal 1085 °C v highest Group 1 metal 181 °C); every transition metal has a higher density (lowest 7.19 v highest 0.97 g/cm³); differences are large, roughly 6 to 30 times for melting point and 7 to 17 times for density; within each set there is variation, for example the transition metal with highest melting point (chromium) has the lowest density; limitation: only three transition metals included, so the claim is supported for these data but more metals should be checked (for example mercury is a liquid); conclusion: the data support the claim.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): uses data to compare both properties, comments on the size of the differences and a limitation, and reaches a conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statement that the data agree, with little use of data.
questions.explanation: Evaluating needs data quoted, a judgement, and a comment on how far the data support a general claim.

questions.question:
A student says: 'Sodium and iron are both metals, so either would be suitable for making the body of a car.'
Evaluate this statement, comparing the properties of sodium and iron.
markScheme: Indicative content: both are metals and conduct electricity and heat, and form positive ions; iron is strong and hard, sodium is soft and can be cut with a knife, so sodium would dent and could not support loads; iron has a high melting point (1538 °C), sodium melts at 98 °C, so sodium would melt near a hot engine; iron has a high density, which gives a solid, rigid body, while sodium is light but too weak; sodium reacts vigorously with water (rain) to form sodium hydroxide and flammable hydrogen, which would be dangerous; sodium tarnishes quickly in air; iron reacts only slowly with oxygen and water (rusts), which can be prevented by painting; conclusion: the statement is wrong, iron (as steel) is suitable and sodium is not, because being a metal does not mean having the same properties.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison of several physical and chemical properties, each linked to suitability, with a clear, justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some comparisons linked to suitability, with a conclusion.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'sodium is reactive', with no clear conclusion.
questions.explanation: Strong answers link each property difference to a consequence for a car body, then make a clear judgement.
